findings.title: Editor backup file `CoreServiceFactory.test.ts-E` committed to the repo
findings.description: The diff adds `packages/core/tests/services/CoreServiceFactory.test.ts-E` — a verbatim copy of the *pre-change* `CoreServiceFactory.test.ts`. It is dead code: it still calls `createContextPipeline(FIXTURE_PROJECT_PATH)` with one argument, which no longer matches the new required `options` parameter (so it would not typecheck if it were ever renamed back to `.ts`), and it will silently drift from the live test file. The `.ts-E` suffix means neither Vitest nor `tsc` picks it up, so nothing in CI flags it. It should be deleted rather than committed.

findings.title: The adoption remedy text and config file name are written out in six places
findings.description:
The same two user-facing strings are re-typed across the module instead of being defined once:
- `.context-forge.toml` is a named constant in `packages/core/src/adoption/adoptionState.ts:8` (`PROJECT_CONFIG_FILE`), but `adoptionResolver.ts:92` hardcodes it inside the error message.
- The "cf config set adoption.state declined" remedy appears in `adoptionResolver.ts:28` (`DECLINE_REMEDY`), `adoptionFacts.ts:93`, `packages/core/src/detection/sourceVolume.ts:36-38` (`OVERRIDE_REMEDY`) and `packages/core/src/detection/planningArtifacts.ts:15-16` (`OVERRIDE_REMEDY`) — the last two with yet different wording.
- The key literal `adoption.state` is defined in `packages/core/src/config/ConfigKeys.ts:112` and again as `ADOPTION_STATE_KEY` in `adoptionState.ts:7`.

This directly contradicts the AGENTS.md rule "Never scatter comparison values across code… Changing a value should require editing exactly one place." A user who renames the key, the file, or the remedy has to find every copy; the two `OVERRIDE_REMEDY` constants already disagree on wording. Exporting one shared remedy constant (and using `PROJECT_CONFIG_FILE` inside it) would remove the duplication.

findings.title: Exported MCP `generateContext` grew a mode parameter in the middle of its signature
findings.description:
`generateContext(projectId, adoptionStateWrites, overrides?, additionalInstructions?, worktreeId?)` now takes five positional parameters, with the new `adoptionStateWrites: AdoptionStateWrites` inserted *before* the three that were already optional. Two consequences:
1. The project's TypeScript rules say "Prefer named parameters (via object destructuring) when a function takes 3+ parameters" — this function is now well past that threshold, and the two call sites (`contextTools.ts:201` and `contextTools.ts:266`) have to remember the order.
2. `generateContext` is an exported function from the MCP package, so inserting a parameter in the middle is a breaking change for any external caller compiled against the previous signature.

An options object (`generateContext(projectId, { adoptionStateWrites, overrides, additionalInstructions, worktreeId })`) would keep the call sites readable and avoid the positional-mode flag.

findings.title: `ContextIntegrator` constructor now takes seven positional parameters
findings.description: The constructor grew from six to seven positional parameters (`resolveAdoptionFn` appended after `resolvePermissivenessFn`), three of which are `null` at most call sites. The new tests make the cost visible: `new ContextIntegrator(engine, true, () => PROFILES, null, null, null, resolver)` — a reader cannot tell which `null` is which without counting. This is the same rule as above ("named parameters … when a function takes 3+ parameters"), and the change makes an existing smell materially worse. Grouping the optional resolvers into a single options object would fix this and the MCP finding together.

findings.title: `cf build` now has an undocumented write side effect
findings.description: `cf build` passes `{ adoptionStateWrites: 'persist' }`, so a Phase 0 build of a detected brownfield project writes `adoption.state = in_progress` into the project's `.context-forge.toml`. The command's own description is still "Generate a context prompt" and the help text does not mention it; the only signal is a bullet inside the generated prompt ("adoption.state was set to in_progress by this build"). The write is clearly intended by the design (and the `cf build --it brownfield-adoption` escape hatch is documented in the error message), but for a command whose output is routinely piped it is worth stating in the command help that Phase 0 builds may persist the adoption state.

findings.title: Parity test's `afterEach` can throw a `TypeError` that masks the real failure
findings.description: `checkout` is declared as `let checkout: string;` and assigned only inside the test body, but `afterEach` unconditionally calls `fs.rmSync(checkout, { recursive: true, force: true })`. If the test fails before that assignment, the cleanup throws `TypeError: The "path" argument must be of type string`, replacing the assertion failure that actually explains the bug. Guarding with `if (checkout)` (and initialising to `undefined`) keeps the original error visible.

findings.title: The comment justifying the `adoption/contracts` import is inaccurate
findings.description: The comment says importing `contracts.ts` "keeps services/ and adoption/ from importing each other's internals", but the adoption module *does* import services internals — `adoption/adoptionResolver.ts:13-15` imports `ContextProfileParser`, `promptFilePath` and `SystemPromptParser` from `../services/`. There is no module cycle (contracts is a leaf), so the design is sound, but the stated reason is wrong and will mislead the next maintainer into thinking the dependency only runs one way.

findings.title: Outcome model is exhaustively typed and fails loudly on an unknown kind
findings.description: `AdoptionOutcome` is a discriminated union, `decideOutcome` is pure and asserts that the facts it needs were supplied ("state is unset, so `artifacts` is required"), and both `isSelected` (`adoptionResolver.ts:52`) and `describeOutcome`/`describeSourceVolume` (`adoptionFacts.ts:41,63`) use `const unhandled: never` so a future outcome kind fails to compile rather than silently falling through. The "never use silent fallback values" rule is respected throughout the new module, including the guide-missing and write-failure paths, which raise `AdoptionError` with a concrete remedy and are rethrown by `ContextIntegrator.generateContextFromProject` (`ContextIntegrator.ts:122`) rather than degrading to the concept prompt.
